transcript: The lack of third spaces in New York City is an epidemic that needs to be studied. pretty much everywhere has some sort of monetary barrier of entry. you know what doesn't though? free Shakespeare in the Park. The Public Theater has been putting on this tradition for decades, and if you've seen this poster around, you might already know that they're making a triumphant return to the renovated Delacorte Theater in Central Park this summer with a production of Twelfth Night. But they also recently wrapped a touring mobile unit production of much ado about nothing and they have a public works production of Pericles coming up at the end of August. last week, they hosted an event at the Fifth Avenue Hotel which included a discussion panel of some folks who've worked on these productions, and at first I wondered if this was just the kind of thing to wine and dine their corporate donors. but the panel was incredible, and there were some really meaningful conversations with these artists and scholars about how their relationships and histories with Shakespeare have shaped their approaches to these productions with the public. ultimately, what surfaced was a deep sense of commitment to making Shakespeare and theatre in general accessible for all New Yorkers and an understanding of just how valuable of a tool that theatre is in building community. I'll just say, if I were there on behalf of a wealthy company or entity, I'd feel pretty good about backing them after experiencing this panel. and then this week I was so fortunate to be at the ribbon cutting ceremony of the renovated Delacorte Theater in Central Park and it was really cool to learn about what went into this massive, multi-million dollar project. we heard some words from some folks of the public and some local government officials who have been heavily involved in this labour of love, and we even got a little Shakespeare from some cast members of Twelfth Night. and then we got to tour the space and we saw firsthand the ways the new Delacorte is more advanced, more weatherproof, and more accessible than ever before. now, I was already a ride or die for the Public's free Shakespeare initiatives, but this really sealed the deal. making these productions completely free and the effort that has been put into making them such a good experience is an act of radical accessibility, and I don't think a lot of casual theatre goers realize just how impactful it is for theatre to be produced in this way. the enthusiasm and diversity that I saw in the audience of much ado when it stopped in my neighbourhood earlier this year was really special, and it just reminded me that theatre is for everyone and there are ways to make theatre community-driven, much like it was originally intended. like, by making it free and showing up to neighbourhoods all over the city, it's not a transaction, it's an offering. and with the public being one of the nation's leading nonprofit theatre companies with I imagine one of the largest operating budgets, it's really nice to see them putting their money where their mouth is and committing to these initiatives. If I haven't yet influenced you let me be clear. I want literally everyone and their mother in New York City to go see twelfth night in Central Park once it begins performances in August. it's being directed by Saheem Ali who recently worked on Buena vista Social Club and Fat Ham, it features an incredible cast including Lupita Nyong’o and Sandra Oh and it is completely free. we need to be showing up in droves, show our gratitude for this even existing, and show that people really want to go to the theatre, if and when it is accessible. with that, I will see you at the Delacorte.
